source_title: Canada sets this condition for international students looking to work there
source_excerpt: Canada's immigration authority has issued a fresh reminder to international students, warning that they can work in the country only if their study permit explicitly allows it and that violating work conditions could have serious consequences, including the loss of student status and possible removal from Canada. In a recent post, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) highlighted key rules that international students must follow while working during their studies. The agency said students can only work in Canada if the conditions listed on their study permit authorize them to work on or off campus. âImportant information for international students who plan to work while studying:â¢ You can only work in Canada as an international student if your study permit conditions say you can.â¢ If you are eligible to work off campus, you can only work up to 24 hours per week while classes are in session.â¢ Working more than you are allowed is a violation of your study permit conditions, which can have serious consequences,â wrote IRCC in a post on X (formerly known as Twitter).What the rules sayIRCCâs guidance says a student can work on or off campus only if the study permit lists a condition allowing it. The department tells students to pay close attention to the number of hours they are allowed to work off campus. A study permit is the document that sets out these terms, and holding one does not give automatic permission to take a job.Study permit must allow workThe immigration department stated that international students are eligible to work in Canada only if their study permit contains a condition permitting on-campus or off-campus employment. Students have been advised to carefully review their permits before accepting any job. IRCC's social media post also reminded students that those eligible to work off campus can work a maximum of 24 hours per week while classes are in session. Working beyond the permitted limit constitutes a violation of study permit conditions.Risk of losing student statusAccording to the agency, students who work more hours than allowed risk losing their student status. The department noted that non-compliance with permit conditions could also affect future applications for study permits or work permits. In some cases, individuals may be required to leave Canada. "Working more hours than you're allowed is a violation of your study permit conditions," IRCC said, adding that students could face consequences if they fail to follow the employment rules attached to their permits.Consequences of working too many hoursAccording to IRCCâs page on unauthorized work, working more than the allowed hours breaches the study permit conditions. A student who does so can lose their student status, and future study or work permit applications may be refused. The student may also have to leave the country.The departmentâs wider warning about unauthorized work, which applies to anyone working in Canada without permission, lists further risks. These include removal from Canada, a permanent record of fraud with IRCC and a five-year ban on returning. Such a record can also hurt the chances of future applications being approved, including for permanent residence. IRCC also says people working without authorisation face greater risks of unsafe conditions, wage theft, abuse and forced or unpaid labour.Working after graduationIRCC says students who want to work after they graduate generally need a work permit, and some are eligible for a post-graduation work permit (PGWP). A graduate who has applied for a PGWP can work full-time while waiting for a decision, but only if certain conditions are met. The applicant must have held a valid study permit when applying, must have completed the program and must have been eligible to work off campus while studying without exceeding the allowed hours. Those who donât meet these conditions must wait for their work permit before starting a new job.Watch for scamsIRCCâs guidance for workers also lists warning signs of immigration fraud, which students may encounter when looking for jobs. These include anyone who promises a work permit or job offer in exchange for payment, asks for documents or payment through social media, or offers free room and board in return for work. IRCC says people who work legally are protected by Canadaâs labour laws and can contact provincial or territorial labour standards offices without their employerâs permission.You use AI every day. en_body:
## Overview of IRCC Guidance

Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has issued a reminder regarding employment rules for international students in Canada. According to the agency's public statements, holding a study permit does not automatically grant permission to take a job. Students must verify that their individual document explicitly authorizes on-campus or off-campus work before accepting any employment.

## Key Employment Rules and Limits

Based on the reported guidance, students who are eligible to work off campus must adhere to specific hour limits while classes are in session.

* **Permit Conditions:** Employment is only permitted if explicitly stated on the study permit.
* **Hour Restrictions:** Eligible students may work up to 24 hours per week off campus during academic sessions.
* **Post-Graduation Work:** Graduates applying for a Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) may have specific provisions allowing them to work full-time while awaiting a decision, provided they met prior study and work eligibility criteria.

## Risks of Non-Compliance

IRCC highlighted that exceeding permitted work hours or working without authorization constitutes a breach of study permit conditions. Reported consequences include:

* Loss of student status.
* Refusal of future study or work permit applications.
* Potential removal from Canada.
* Broader risks associated with unauthorized labor, including potential records of non-compliance.

## Verification and Official Resources

Prospective and current international students are advised to consult official channels to verify permit conditions, tuition requirements, and immigration policies. Exact institutional policies, program structures, and application steps vary by designated learning institution (DLI).

To review official policies and verify announcements, applicants should consult the official [IRCC website](https://www.canada.ca/en/immigration-refugees-citizenship.html). Admission, scholarships, and visas are never guaranteed and depend entirely on individual assessments by Canadian immigration authorities and educational institutions.
